Namyslow Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Namysłów, Poland

Not demolished. Jews are first recorded in Namysłów in 1321; expelled in 1582, they returned in 1683. Population grew from 40 (1.6%) in 1787 to 174 by 1845, then declined sharply through westward emigration to just 68 by 1932. Kristallnacht saw the synagogue burned and Jewish shops destroyed; only 16 Jews remained after 1939, their fate afterward unknown. This cemetery received an 1792 building permit and was established in 1794 on the so-called Polish Manor grounds, fenced in 1862 with a funeral house added. During Kristallnacht, broken matzevot were displayed on stakes at the entrance as a further act of desecration; in 1939 ownership transferred to the Reich Association of Jews in Germany, and the site was fully liquidated during WWII, replaced by forced-laborer and POW barracks, a building-materials warehouse, and a cattle market. Eyewitnesses recall tombstones surviving until the 1960s, when the cemetery was completely destroyed; the land became private property in the 1970s. A 1986 heating-network excavation uncovered two unidentifiable metal coffins, later reburied in the municipal cemetery.
